Right: the same graph with the edge between B and C reversed, which creates the cycle B, E, C, B (shown in the accent color), so is_dag() returns False." width="100%"} A DAG is a directed graph with no directed cycles: there is no way to follow edges in their direction and return to the node you started from. The check runs a depth-first search over the whole graph and reports a cycle as soon as it finds an edge leading back to a node still on the current search path. It takes time linear in the number of nodes plus edges. A self-loop is a cycle of length one, so any self-loop makes the result `False`. The graph doesn't need to be connected, and the current selection is ignored. DAGs model anything with a "must come before" relationship, so this check is useful for: - validating dependency graphs (packages, build targets, task pipelines) before ordering them - confirming that a citation, version, or causal graph has no circular references - guarding calls that require acyclic input, such as `topological_sort()` If the result is `False`, `simple_cycles()` can help locate the offending cycles. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph has no directed cycles, `False` if it contains at least one. A directed graph with no edges is a DAG. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on an undirected graph. Note that `ec.Graph()` is undirected by default, so create the graph with `directed=True` to use this method. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A simple chain `A -> B -> C` has no way back to its start, so it is a DAG: ::: {#53c0a257 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.is_dag() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Adding an edge back from "C" to "A" closes the loop `A -> B -> C -> A`, so the graph is no longer acyclic: ::: {#3a101ff7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("C", "A") graph.is_dag() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Acyclic is not the same as tree-shaped. In this small build pipeline, "test" and "docs" both depend on "compile", and "release" depends on both of them. The two routes from "compile" to "release" form a diamond, but there is no directed cycle, so the pipeline is still a valid DAG: ::: {#bfbf4695 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pipeline = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["compile", "test", "docs", "release"]) .add_edges( [ ("compile", "test"), ("compile", "docs"), ("test", "release"), ("docs", "release"), ] ) ) pipeline.is_dag() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
